newsitem.title: UK: Labour govt to unveil first UK budget July 2.
newsitem.headline: Labour govt to unveil first UK budget July 2.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government will have a chance to demonstrate just how radical it intends to be when it presents its first budget on Wednesday, July 2.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown announced the date on Monday, breaking the recent tradition of holding budgets on a Tuesday to avoid a clash with the handover of Hong Kong from Britain to China.

Brown, who stunned financial markets within days of taking office last month by giving the Bank of England freedom to set interest rates, has said the theme of his first budget would be "welfare-to-work."

The centrepiece will be a "windfall" tax on the profits of privatised utility companies, expected to raise three to five billion pounds ($5-7.5 billion) which will be used to create work for 250,000 young and long-term unemployed people.
Prime Minister Tony Blair said on Monday that the welfare system had to be reformed to help people help themselves, while providing for those who could not.
The government also wanted to encourage people like single mothers to get back into employment.
"This is empowerment, not punishment," Blair said.

The chancellor again demonstrated his boldness on Monday by appointing two foreign economists -- American DeAnne Julius and Dutchman Willem Buiter -- to the new monetary policy committee at the Bank of England which will set interest rates.

Other outside members will be Professor Charles Goodhart and Sir Alan Budd, chief economic adviser to the Treasury. The four Bank of England representatives, led by central Bank Governor Eddie George, had already been named.
As Brown prepares the first budget from a Labour government in 19 years, the main question in most economists' minds is not whether he will increase taxes but by how much.
Although the public finances are in reasonably good shape, economists say some increase in taxes is necessary to dampen runaway consumer spending and prevent a resurgence in inflation.

Brown must perform a difficult balancing act, keeping Labour's election promise not to raise the tax burden on ordinary people while demonstrating that the party can make a difference to unemployment and the quality of key public services -- all while keeping financial markets happy.
If Brown can also persuade the Bank of England that he is doing something to dampen consumer demand, this could reduce the extent of the monetary tightening which also appears inevitable.

The new Chancellor's Bank of England reforms made it clear that he is not afraid of radical moves and raise the possibility that the first full Labour budget since April 1978 may be more far-reaching than financial markets expect.
However, the fact that Brown will have had little time to prepare for his first big moment at the despatch box could suggest a more modest package is likely.

Brown limited his room for manoeuvre before the May 1 election by promising not to increase the standard or top rates of income tax and to live within tight spending limits set by his Conservative predecessor Kenneth Clarke.
Nevertheless, Roger Bootle and Jonathan Loynes of HSBC Markets say there is little the Chancellor cannot do and there are hundreds of tax reliefs and allowances he could target.

"The pre-election promises not to raise the basic and higher rates of income tax do not bind Mr Brown's hands to any significant extent -- after all the last government enacted a huge fiscal tightening in the two 1993 budgets without touching either of those rates," they wrote in their budget study.
Brown's only other firm promise was not to extend value-added tax to food, children's clothes, books or public transport.
"From a macro-economic point of view, it makes most sense to target the personal sector, since this is the side of the economy which needs cooling down," Bootle and Loynes wrote.
Many analysts expect a cut in advance corporation tax (ACT), which, perversely, raises revenue by reducing the tax credits companies receive on dividend payments.

If he wants to maintain his reputation for radicalism, Brown may make some move towards introducing a 10 percent starting rate of income tax, although this would have to be offset by extra revenue from elsewhere.

Tax relief on personal allowances could be limited to the basic rate of income tax, now 23 percent, instead of the top rate of 40 percent, raising around two billion pounds of revenue to compensate for the 10 percent rate.
Tax relief on mortgage interest payments is expected to be reduced or abolished outright, a move that would hit millions of people in this nation of home-owners.
